title: 77% of Indian Companies Plan to Expand Global Hiring, Willing to Pay Premium for Top Talent
excerpt: A Deel survey of over 1,000 senior leaders finds Indian businesses are hiring abroad for specialized skills, not cost savings, with North America as the top destination.
body:
• 77% of Indian companies plan to increase global hiring over the next 12–18 months, according to a Deel survey of 1,008 senior decision-makers across seven Indian cities.
  • Access to specialized talent (34%) has overtaken cost savings as the top reason for hiring internationally, with 89% of companies seeking advanced technology and engineering roles abroad.
  • North America is the top destination for Indian companies' global workforces (36%), ahead of Europe/UK (27%) and APAC (21%).
  • Compliance — not cost — is the biggest barrier, with 76% of companies citing regulatory and administrative burden as their primary challenge in scaling globally.

More than three-quarters of Indian companies plan to expand their overseas hiring over the next 12 to 18 months, according to a new survey by global HR platform Deel — a signal that India's corporate ambitions are no longer confined to serving foreign clients from Indian offices but increasingly involve building workforces across borders.

The survey, which polled 1,008 senior decision-makers and HR leaders across seven major Indian cities, found that global hiring has become a mainstream strategy. More than half of the companies surveyed already have over a quarter of their workforce based outside India, and 58% operate in four or more countries. Nearly one in five operates across more than 10.

Paying More for the Right Skills

The data challenges the longstanding assumption that Indian companies expand overseas to cut costs. Just 34% of respondents cited access to specialized or emerging skills as their primary reason for hiring globally, while 33% pointed to the need to be closer to customers and local markets. Another 20% said they hire internationally to run 24/7 operations.

The demand is heaviest in technology. Nearly nine in ten companies hiring globally (89%) are seeking advanced technology and engineering talent — core developers, AI and machine learning specialists, and R&D professionals. Sales and business development roles follow at 80%, with product and design at 45%.

"India's economic momentum, maturing startup ecosystem, thriving digital economy, and increasingly supportive policy environment are giving Indian companies the confidence to build globally, not just serve global clients from India."

— Rakesh Gaur, Head of Sales for India at Deel

North America remains the top destination, cited by 36% of respondents, ahead of Europe and the UK (27%) and APAC (21%). The preference for high-income markets underscores that Indian employers are willing to pay more to hire talent that directly influences product roadmaps and revenue.

Compliance Is the Real Bottleneck

If talent is pulling Indian companies abroad, compliance is slowing them down. Three-quarters (76%) of respondents named compliance and administrative burden — not the cost of expansion — as their primary challenge. Navigating global payroll, local tax laws, statutory benefits, and risks such as worker misclassification and permanent establishment topped the list of concerns.

Only one in ten companies said they were highly confident their global HR and payroll setup was fully compliant. Among companies that experienced delays in global expansion, local entity setup taking longer than expected was the leading cause (42%), followed by visa and immigration delays (31%) and payroll or tax filing errors (27%).

The business impact is tangible. Seven in ten companies said compliance delays had pushed back a product or market launch. Nearly six in ten experienced delayed revenue because new hires were not productive on time, and 49% lost or delayed a deal, contract, or project.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indian professionals based in North America, Europe, and other high-income markets, the trend is a potential tailwind. As Indian companies move from outsourcing models to building genuine global teams, diaspora professionals with dual cultural fluency — understanding both Indian business culture and local market norms — are positioned to benefit. The survey suggests employers are not just filling roles abroad but investing in talent that can shape strategy and drive growth from international hubs.

The Rise of Employer of Record

To manage the complexity, 34% of companies have adopted an Employer of Record model, which allows them to hire in foreign markets without establishing a local entity. Another 24% use a mix of EOR, contractors, and owned entities depending on the country and role. Among EOR adopters, 40% say the model saves both time and cost, while 35% say it primarily saves time.

"Indian companies want to scale globally, but managing compliance across fragmented systems isn't just inefficient — it's a compliance liability," Gaur said. "The ones that win will consolidate their operations onto a platform built for global growth."
